Bernanos’s polemic in La France contre les Robots (1946) is thoroughly old-fashioned and ineffective.
Its manner is the same polemical hissing we find in Theodor Haecker’s Satire and Polemic, which could still make an impression thirty years ago.
As for its substance, it is a critique of the technological age of a kind we in Germany have known since the beginning of the century through Max Weber, Troeltsch, and Rathenau.

And in the end the author reveals himself as a respectable anti-Vichy man, which means he can be certain of a license from the present regime. He spits on the poor French policeman of 1940, who behaved in a perfectly ordinary way. It is embarrassing: the excited polemic of a man who emigrated in good time and in complete comfort, who never spent a single day in prison and never lived through a bombing raid, and who now comes back to beat us Europeans over the head with his standards.
The old ghosts that cannot die are happy to forgive. But they cannot forget.
To be unable to die means: to be unable to forget.
An inability to grant amnesty. They want to go on living. They do not even want merely to survive.
This Karl Barth really has no more to do with the Christ of the reborn human being than any pope—or, for that matter, Pope Joan.

“If I had the misfortune to be German, I freely admit that at Munich, standing before Daladier and Chamberlain, the two Big Men of that time, I would have been tempted to think myself not merely a lord, but God.”
So says Georges Bernanos in La France contre les Robots—robot = machine!!—1946, p. 173.
In chaos, nothing remains to us except the discernment of spirits.
How else could a cosmos ever arise? But to discern the spirits already means distinguishing friend from enemy.
Anything else would be a joke.
From Henri Murger to Henry Miller.
Henry Miller’s Tropic of Cancer is Henri Murger’s Bohemia all over again.
Instead of Alsatians, we now have Americans, and the whole thing is filled with global human types.

The Priapism is open. So is the despair. It no longer ties a little pink ribbon around itself. It shamelessly admits what it is and even manages to draw a certain spiritual impulse from that shamelessness.
“The whole earth staggering with crime and distress.”
“Man has been betrayed because he calls upon the best part of his nature, and that is all” (p. 121).
We heard this back in 1840 as well. But only now, after the Second World War, is it finally being carried through consistently—and globally.
The line of development from 1848 to 1948 runs from the proletariat to the peripsēma—the cast-off refuse. That is the whole of progress.
I said that despair no longer ties a little pink ribbon around itself.
In the second half of Henry Miller’s book, a hymn to humanity appears.
More precisely, it is a hymn to the art of Matisse, in which the flesh breathes so beautifully.
A tremendous relief: from the variété de la pâture sexuelle, the variety of sexual fodder, to the variété de la pâture culturelle et humanitaire, the variety of cultural and humanitarian fodder.
The paralyzing legend: the white gods who come from the East.
The line from 1848 to 1948 is the development and intensification of nothingness and nihilism.
Put in concrete sociological terms: from the proletariat to the peripsēma.
Existentialist chatter accompanies the crossing over into the shamelessness of nothingness.
The Christian peripsēma seems to have been used up.
The German would rather be a criminal than a citizen?
But he did not want to be a proletarian either. So instead he flew into a rage and became a Hitlerian.
I fear that he will fly into an even worse rage once he grasps the idea of the peripsēma.
Only then will we really see the Antichrist.
Compared with the peripsēma, the proletarian is merely an ambitious climber on the ladder of historical development.
Today the enemy is the non-nothing. And that is precisely the Christian.
In W. Grewe’s publications on occupation law, the basic fact always remains the same: the situation of the defeated party in a discriminatory world war.

May Herbert Krüger’s excellent essay in Gegenwart (September 1948) help the Third World War return to a human concept of the enemy. But the Furies of the just war have now been unleashed, and they will probably not be so easy to tame again.

Until that happens, everything constructed as “law” must end up serving the right and advantage of the side that wages the just war, as one can already read in Vitoria. And our entire situation—constitution, Basic Law, occupation statute—remains one gigantic versari in re illicita: existence within an unlawful situation.
At last time makes Saul Too weak and tired to persecute.

After four years of occupation, the animus hostilis—the hostile intention—must surely have worn itself down somewhat, and the provisional arrangement must surely begin to stabilize in one direction or another.
Perhaps even the tu quoque—“you did it too”—will eventually gain a little room for use against our guardians and educators.

In any case, Grewe’s scholarly achievement in international law is extraordinary. He is now Germany’s leading teacher of international law. That is not merely an achievement and a task. It is also a situation.
May every good spirit assist him in it. These victors are not even capable of establishing a clear spatial order for the earth.
Henry Miller has discovered him and sounded the alarm: the friends of classical education, the lovers of the past.
“There is something obscene in this love of the past,” he says.
“Something obscene in all this spiritual commotion that allows a cretin to sprinkle holy water on Big Berthas, dreadnoughts, and explosives.”
And now it comes, on p. 303—the great killing potential of a new persecution:
“Anyone with a belly full of the classics is an enemy of the human race!”
The phrase enemy of the human race has by now become more explosive than any atomic bomb or biological weapon, even if it begins merely as a slogan.
Someone will always come along who takes it seriously.
“The world looks more and more like an entomologist’s dream.”

At the end, looking at the Seine flowing quietly, he writes:

So, in the end: space after all.
Taken as a whole: rotten flesh prepared with literary nonchalance.
Spirit serves as seasoning so that one can swallow the stinking flesh.
The result is a myth of blood and excrement whose potential for killing is considerable.
“In the face of the field of ruins.”

That is how the Bavarian Constitution of 26 October 1946 begins, documenting the fact that even the Bavarians, standing before a landscape of ruins, could think of nothing better than cheap, moldy banalities left over from the good old age of constitutionalism.
Perhaps the relationship between cat and mouse is itself only the outcome of a very long war.
Perhaps it is simply the permanent fixing of that war’s result.
As Heraclitus says: war makes some free and others slaves.
In this way it has made some beings and others mice. It reveals nature—physis—and at the same time fixes it in place. That is the justice of war. That is natural law.
War between human beings still has its honor. It is not just.
Only war between natural beings is just. It ends by revealing that some are free and others slaves, some cats and others mice.
Law is the final distribution of space.
Law is first of all division and distribution—and specifically the division and distribution of land.
Law is the clear distribution of freedom and subjection.
We jurists, after all, are only scribes. We do not possess the Word directly. We do not possess the image directly. We possess only writing.
We can count ourselves lucky if we are at least the first to write something down ourselves—as with so-called customary law—instead of being forced to rewrite a law that has already been written.
On Annie Kraus’s book On Stupidity (Carolus Verlag Knecht, Frankfurt):
On p. 38 of Annie Kraus’s “stupidity,” one comes across my name.
Identity and continuity cannot be disputed, so the recommendation to the prosecutors—on p. 42 I am called “co-responsible”—lands concretely enough.

What I now read in print from Annie Kraus—while remembering, with some emotion, her doe-eyed look—is much the same as what I heard from Kempner’s own mouth. But Kempner and I managed to have a conversation.
